beats: Hook (line_qc_sw_same_piano): same chip, same program, two compilers: one output is the answer, the other is noise. Same piano, same sheet, two players. Cast for all of QC01 (the six parts cut from her first lecture, Q25-01): the physicist (older, bald with a fluffy fringe, bushy moustache, goggles pushed up, lab coat) and the student (lanky, a tuft of hair, round glasses, striped long-sleeved T-shirt, messenger bag); both invented. No lecturer figure anywhere and never her likeness: her voice and her slides carry her part. Here the physicist stands for hardware, the student for software.

The matmul ladder (tape p13 and keep its "Charles Leiserson, MIT 6.172" credit): Python loops, Java, C, optimisation flags, parallel loops, vectorisation: 53,292x on the same CPU (check: MIT 6.172 Fall 2018 lecture 1; Science 2020 has 62,806x for a newer setup: say which). Reuse line_cluster_stairs or line_tiles_staircase as the staircase; code draws the bars on a log scale.
Why the first step is so slow: plain Python is translated word by word as it runs; C is translated once, ahead of time (line_qc_sw_live_interpreter).
"You cannot imagine a human programming in binary" (clip 61:17-61:40; line_qc_sw_switch_wall).
A quantum program: wires are qubits, layers of two-qubit gates (tape p14 with the chip photo covered; code draws the circuit).

Noise caps program size, like the tide caps a sandcastle; with software optimisation about 2x larger programs still give usable answers (line_qc_sw_tide_castles; her report of IBM collaborators' data: attribute it, do not present it as published).
Half of the decade's gain in runnable circuit size from hardware, half from software (clip 64:26-64:51; line_qc_sw_tandem; reuse line_balance).
As hardware grows more complex, software matters more (line_qc_sw_pipe_organ; clip 59:16-59:52).

Cover (line_qc_cover_01_05; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): the physicist and the student pedal one tandem uphill, a tiny chip riding in the basket. Clips start after 59:16 (57:54-59:16 is on the syllabus avoid list: never used).
